teaser: Designed over Christmas by an unknown illustrator, it made Paris stop in the street.
review_notes:
Standard account (largely from Mucha's own telling): he was at the Lemercier printing works over Christmas 1894 when Sarah Bernhardt asked for a new poster; it appeared on Paris walls on 1 January 1895 for the revival opening 4 January.
The palm branch refers to the Palm Sunday procession in the play's last act.
Collectors bribing bill posters or cutting posters off walls: widely repeated anecdote.
The plain lower part is often explained by lack of time.
Six-year contract with Bernhardt. Poster approx. 216 x 74 cm, printed in two sheets (join visible near mid-height in this image).
The printer's manager reportedly disliked the design at first.

lesson.text: A procession is passing. A woman in a heavy embroidered robe has stopped mid-step, a palm branch held upright in one hand, the other hand pressed to her chest. Her eyes are lifted toward something you cannot see. Nothing in this image moves, and nothing is about to.

She is Sarah Bernhardt, the most famous actress in the world in 1894, in the last act of a play called Gismonda. She plays a duchess of medieval Athens walking in a Palm Sunday procession. It is the solemn high point of the evening, and the poster holds it still.

Paris posters of the 1890s did the opposite. They shouted: dancers kicking, bright reds and yellows, a joke you got in one second from a passing carriage. This one whispers, and its shape alone was strange.
Start with the format, because that was the first shock.

lines.label: One long vertical
lines.text: The sheet is about 2.16 meters tall and only 74 centimeters wide (roughly 7 feet by 2.5). The actress appears close to life size, like a person standing in a doorway.

lines.label: The arch
lines.text: A round arch of mosaic curves behind her head and carries the letters of her name. It works like a halo around a saint in a church.

lines.label: The join
lines.text: A faint horizontal seam crosses the image here. The poster was too tall for one sheet, so it was printed in two halves and pasted together on the wall.

lesson.text: A tall niche, a halo, a figure in ceremonial dress: Mucha borrowed the language of religious art to sell theater tickets. Bernhardt's fans called her “the divine Sarah”. He simply took them at their word.

Mucha was not supposed to get this job. By his own account he was at the Lemercier printing works over the Christmas holidays, checking proofs as a favor, when Bernhardt called needing a poster in a hurry. Every regular artist was away. He was 34 and almost unknown.

The technique is color lithography: the drawing is made on flat stones, one stone for each color, and the sheet goes through the press once per stone. Mucha chose soft colors, such as pale gold, sage green, pink and powder blue, where others used primaries.

lesson.title: From head to hem
lesson.text: Follow the figure down, the way a passerby's eye would have.

spots.title: The profile
spots.text: Her face is turned up and away, mouth slightly open, under a huge crown of pink orchids. Orange hair falls behind her shoulder. She does not look at the public at all.

spots.title: The palm
spots.text: A tall green palm branch, cut out against bare paper, rises higher than her head. It is the sign of Palm Sunday, and its long stem repeats the tall format of the sheet.

spots.title: The hand on the chest
spots.text: Her left hand spreads over a jeweled collar and a stiff, gold-embroidered mantle. The fabric is drawn with a dark outline, then filled with flat pattern.

spots.title: The robe
spots.text: A pale blue-green dress scrolls with golden plants and flowers and falls in one unbroken column. The body nearly vanishes: what you see is line and ornament.

lesson.text: That strong outline filled with flat pattern, the long flowing hair, the plants turning into decoration: within a year or two Parisians had a name for it, “le style Mucha”. Today we file it under Art Nouveau, the “new art” of curving, plant-like lines that spread across Europe around 1900.
Gismonda proved that an advertisement could be quiet, tall and elegant, and stop people more surely than a loud one.
The posters went up on January 1, 1895. Collectors wanted them so badly that some reportedly bribed the men who pasted them, and others went out at night with razors to cut them off the walls.
Not everything is solemn. Mucha was working against a deadline, and the lower part of the sheet is much emptier than the top. But he did hide someone down there.
The actress is not the only person on this poster. Where is the other one?

spots.title: The little bearer
spots.text: Just above the words “Théâtre de la Renaissance”, a small crouching man with a wide-eyed face peers over the banner he is holding up with both hands.

lesson.text: Around him you can read the practical information the whole image exists for: the theater's name on the scroll, the printer's name in tiny capitals along the bottom edge, and “Mucha” signed at the lower left.
Bernhardt liked the result so much that she signed Mucha to a six-year contract. He went on to design her posters, and also stage sets, costumes and jewelry.

The frozen instant turned out to be a beginning. The unknown illustrator who filled in over Christmas spent the next decade as the most imitated designer in Paris, and the woman under the arch kept her halo on every poster he made for her.

quiz.question: What moment of the play does the poster show?
options: A duel in the first act
A Palm Sunday procession in the last act
quiz.explanation: Bernhardt, as Gismonda, walks in the Palm Sunday procession holding a palm.

quiz.question: Why is there a faint horizontal seam across the middle?
options: The poster was printed in two sheets joined together
quiz.explanation: At over two meters tall, it was too long for a single sheet.

quiz.question: What does the mosaic arch behind her head resemble?
quiz.explanation: Mucha borrowed the look of religious images for “the divine Sarah”.

quiz.question: What is color lithography?
options: Printing from flat stones, one stone per color
quiz.explanation: The sheet passes through the press once for each color stone.

quiz.question: What did Sarah Bernhardt do after seeing the poster?
options: She gave Mucha a six-year contract
She asked for a different artist
quiz.explanation: He went on to design posters, sets, costumes and jewelry for her.

facts.text: Mucha was already the most famous poster artist in Paris when he got the Gismonda job.
facts.explanation: He was 34 and almost unknown, filling in over the holidays.

facts.text: On the poster, Bernhardt looks straight out at the passersby.
facts.explanation: She is in profile, eyes lifted upward and away.

facts.text: A small crouching figure holds up the banner with the theater's name.
facts.explanation: He peers over the scroll near the bottom of the sheet.
